Renting the Red House in Bridgehampton

Elaine and Bill, with Sander and Kline, rent the “Red House,” a modest Victorian house; a life of continual parties with the twins Joan and Nancy Ward, New York friends, local pubs, beaches, and hangovers.
Summer 1954: the de Koonings, now leading relatively independent lives, share the Red House with Kline, Sander, and Ward.
the Hellmans' quarters, BMC

Olson founds the magazine and invites Creeley as editor, to signal the college's viability amid worries about its future and to show its reorientation from the visual arts toward the literary and dramatic arts. The magazine fails to save the college but succeeds in embodying its literary reorientation.

Frustrated by the piecemeal publication of their work, Olson and Creeley first turn to Cid Corman's Origin and Jonathan Williams's Jargon, then, unhappy with their lack of control, create their own publication, the Black Mountain Review, of considerable later influence. The students print their own texts: Joel Oppenheimer (Sad Devil Press), Nick Cernovich (Black Mountain Graphics Workshop), Stan Vanderbeek (One Thumb Press, which never printed anything), Tommy Jackson (Grapnel Press).

A magazine edited by Creeley; seven issues, an influence out of proportion to its short life; it explains why “Black Mountain poetry” is still regarded as a movement comparable to the Imagists or the Beats.
Discovering the first issue of the Black Mountain Review
Creeley brings in his luggage, by ship from Spain, the first issue of the Black Mountain Review, printed cheaply there.

In no. 3 of the Black Mountain Review (fall 1954), Duncan publishes his letters for Levertov; a passage (“knockd me over with a feather weight of words”) may have been taken as mockery of her work, starting a correspondence that flourished into the 1960s.
